application_credentials.description:
Nothing is needed here: the integration signs in with its own Cloudflare OAuth client.

Add a credential only if you want to use [your own OAuth client]({docs_oauth_clients}) instead. Create it under Manage Account → OAuth clients with the redirect URL `{redirect_uri}`, the grant types authorization code and refresh token, token endpoint authentication set to none (PKCE), and the scopes {scopes}. Then enter its client ID and leave the secret empty. The [project notes]({more_info_url}) explain each step.

user.title: Cloudflare Access
user.description:
Cloudflare Access will protect the whole hostname.

People with a Home Assistant account log in through Access, and voice assistants or MCP clients get their tokens from Access too.

On the next page you sign in with Cloudflare. The consent page lists the permissions the integration uses.

Please use a desktop browser: the Android companion app cannot complete the return from the consent page.

account.title: Cloudflare account
account.description:
The sign-in covers several accounts.

Choose the one whose zone serves the hostname.

api_token.title: Cloudflare API token
api_token.description:
An account-level API token; it is stored in the config entry.

It needs the permissions 'Access: Apps and Policies: Edit' and 'Access: Organizations, Identity Providers, and Groups: Read'; 'Access: Service Tokens: Edit' for script clients, 'Access: Organizations: Revoke' to log removed people out, and 'Access: Audit Logs: Read' for the login history.

settings.title: Hostname and options
settings.description:
Cloudflare Access will guard {hostname}, the hostname of your External URL.

Nothing changes at the edge until you enable it in the options, so you can prepare the settings first.

data.delete_objects_on_remove: Delete the Access applications when the integration is removed

data_description.session_duration: How long a login lasts before the person has to log in again: an [Access session]({docs_session}) in the browser, and the login a client holds, of either kind.
data_description.delete_objects_on_remove:
When the integration is removed, its Access applications are removed too.

Turn this off to keep them in Cloudflare, for example so another instance can adopt them.

people.name: People
people.description:
Access lets in every person who has an e-mail address below.

If a person's login username is an e-mail address, it is used as is. For anyone else, type an address here; without one, the person cannot log in.{no_address_note}

bypass.name: Bypass policies
bypass.description:
Bypass policies let some requests through without a login.

They are for callers that cannot hold the login cookie or a token, for example a third-party service posting to a webhook, or a media player fetching audio by URL. Nothing is open unless it is listed here.

data_description.extra_bypass_paths:
Path prefixes that anyone can reach without logging in.

Each one becomes an [Access bypass policy]({docs_policies}). The list offers what this Home Assistant serves; you can also type any prefix.

reauth_confirm.title: Sign in with Cloudflare again
reauth_confirm.description:
Cloudflare no longer accepts the sign-in, or the sign-in lacks a permission the integration uses: reading the login history, or ending the sessions of removed people.

On the next page you sign in again and grant everything the integration uses.

abort.no_external_url: Home Assistant has no External URL, so there is no hostname to guard. Set it under [Settings, System, Network]({docs_external_url}), then add the integration again.

middleware_unavailable.title: Clients authenticated by Cloudflare Access cannot be recognised
middleware_unavailable.description:
Home Assistant's web server did not accept the integration's authentication hook, so requests from token-bearing clients (Google Assistant, Alexa, MCP clients) that Cloudflare Access let through are rejected by Home Assistant.

This follows a change in Home Assistant's web server library that the integration does not know yet. Report it with your Home Assistant version; a restart does not help.

no_allowed_users.title: No Home Assistant user can pass the Cloudflare Access gate
no_allowed_users.description:
No person has an e-mail address any more, so there is nobody to put in the gate's allow policy.

The policy keeps its last entries. Enter an address under the integration's options, People, or [change a username]({docs_change_username}) to the address.

person.title: Let {email} in
person.description:
Someone logged in as {email} on {when} and was turned away from {app}, because the address is not on the allow list.

If this is a person of the household, pick them: the address becomes their login e-mail and the gate lets it in from the next reload. Otherwise ignore this issue; the attempt got nowhere.

abort.no_people: There is no person to give the address to.

mcp_auth_conflict.title: HA-MCP's login mode does not work behind Cloudflare Access

init.title: Settle HA-MCP's login against the gate
init.description:
HA-MCP is in its {mode} mode, so it asks for its own login on its webhook, while Cloudflare Access asks for a login first. A client can pass only one, so connections fail.

Choose which login remains on the webhook.

menu_options.secret_url: Switch HA-MCP to its secret URL mode: the Access login is the credential, the URL a second factor
menu_options.bypass: List the webhook under Bypass policies: HA-MCP's own login stays the only gate there

no_external_url.title: Home Assistant's External URL is gone

url.title: Set the External URL
url.description:
The Cloudflare Access gate guards the hostname of Home Assistant's External URL, and there is none any more. The applications stay as they were.

Enter the public https URL of Home Assistant; the gate follows its hostname. It can also be set under [Settings, System, Network]({docs_external_url}).

error.invalid_url: Enter an https URL with a hostname.

initiate_flow.user: Add an app that registers itself

user.title: An app that registers itself
user.description: e.g. Claude, ChatGPT. It finds the login on its own and registers with the gate ([managed OAuth]({docs_managed_oauth})); nothing is created for it, only its callback URL is allowed. Removing it stops new logins at once; a login it already holds lasts until the session duration runs out.

data_description.name: A name that identifies the app to you. e.g. Claude, ChatGPT.
data_description.redirect_uris: The URL the app returns to after the login. The list offers the published callbacks of the apps that register themselves; any other URL can be typed, and {example_wildcard_redirect} covers every path under a host.

reconfigure.title: Change the app
reconfigure.description: Saving updates the callback URLs the gate lets the app register with.

user.title: A script or service with its own credentials
user.description: e.g. a backup job, a monitoring probe on another machine. It runs with nobody behind it and gets [an Access service token]({docs_service_tokens}) to send with every request; the next page shows it. Removing it deletes the token.

data_description.name: A name that identifies the script to you. e.g. Backup job.

reconfigure.title: Change the script
reconfigure.description:
Saving renames the token and extends its validity.

The next page shows the credentials again.

data_description.name: A name that identifies the script to you. e.g. Backup job.

credentials.title: Credentials for {name}
credentials.description:
Enter these in the script.

It sends them as the request headers `CF-Access-Client-Id` and `CF-Access-Client-Secret`, together with its usual Home Assistant token ([how service tokens work]({docs_service_tokens})). They are valid until {expires_at}; reconfigure the script to extend that. The secret is shown only here and when you reconfigure the script.

Client ID: `{client_id}`

Client secret: `{client_secret}`
